dataFragment.data:
You may have heard that the beach near that village, not far from here, had its own, darker history.
A hush falls over the table. For a moment, the sound of the sea seems to recede, replaced by a heavy, shared silence. The name hangs in the air between them.
Rahel: (She finally speaks, her voice quieter now, stripped of its earlier vigor) Tantura... the name brings a bitter taste. We heard the rumors in the Valley, even during the fighting. A hard battle. A village that refused to surrender. A village that... men who fought for the Alexandroni Brigade did... things. We didn't want to believe it. It didn't fit our narrative of the pure, righteous defense of our new life. After the war, when my friend was helping build the resort industry here, we would drive up the coast. We would pass the new kibbutz, Nahsholim, that was built on Tantura's land, with the beautiful beach and the old limestone quarry. My friend's inn was just down the road. She would always get quiet. She would never say a word against the army, against the state. But I knew.

There was a shame there. For years, we all pushed it away. It was an unfortunate, unavoidable side effect of a harsh war. It was an aberration. A rogue unit. But now... now the testimonies of those soldiers are being published. The "new historians" are writing about it. It's a wound that will not heal because it was never properly cleaned. It festered. We, the pioneers, built our state on a dream of purity and justice. Tantura reminds us that no human enterprise, not even one as divinely inspired as ours, is untainted by the mud of sin. To acknowledge it fully is to have to re-evaluate the price of our miracle.
Yonatan: (He scoffs, the sound sharp and dismissive) Tantura. Of course, it's the left's favorite whipping boy. A "dark history." Let's be clear. Tantura was a hostile Arab village. Its men fought alongside the Iraqi forces that invaded our country. They sat on a strategic point on the coast. The Alexandroni Brigade was given orders to take it. When an enemy village resists, and your own men are dying, there are consequences. These were Arab

soldiers in civilian clothes, irregulars who did not respect the rules of war, and they paid the price. War is not a classroom debate. Some villages fled, like Lydda and Ramle, and no one calls those roads a crime. Some fought, like Tantura. They lost. Are there claims of a massacre? Yes. Have they been "proven"? No. It's hearsay, propaganda, fueled by our enemies and by self-hating Israelis like Benny Morris who want to deconstruct our own legitimacy. Let me tell you what the real "dark history" is. The real dark history is the pogroms of 1929 in Hebron and Safed, where Jews were slaughtered by their Arab neighbors. The real dark history is the Arab Legion's massacre of our nurses on the road to Mount Scopus. But those are acceptable crimes. Our supposed crimes are unforgivable. I see Tantura not as a source of shame, but as a brutal necessity. The "darkest history" would have been our failure to take that village. The darkest history would have been more of our soldiers dying for the sake of "playing nice" in a war to the death. We did what we had to

do to secure this beach, this resort, this state. I feel no guilt. I feel only frustration that we are even still talking about it.
David: Tantura... In my community, we didn't know the name at the time. We were in Iraq, fighting our own battle for survival. But when I came here, I heard the whispers. And to me, it was not a surprise. It was... a grim echo. In Iraq, we lived amongst Arabs for centuries. We knew them. We knew their honor, their hospitality. We also knew their brutality, their capacity for mob violence. That is the truth of human beings. Both sides have that capacity. When I hear about Tantura, I hear a story of Jews and Arabs caught in the vortex of 1948. I do not trust the official Israeli story that it was merely a clean battle. I have seen too much state-sponsored denial regarding the treatment of Mizrahi Jews to be so naive. But I also do not trust the Palestinian narrative that it was a simple, one-sided slaughter. Because I also know the Arab militias. I know how they fought. I see in Tantura the perfect symbol of the tragedy. Not a unique

atrocity, but a representative one. Arab villagers resisted the new state they refused to accept. Jewish soldiers, scarred by war and filled with fear and perhaps vengeance, were ordered to remove that resistance. And in that awful intersection, people died, some combatants, some perhaps not. It was not just about "our" side being righteous. It was about two peoples fighting over one land, and in such a fight, humanity is the first casualty. What pains me most is what was lost. A fishing village. A place where people had lived for generations. Under Ottoman rule, under the British. Their history erased. Their mosque destroyed. And for what? For a kibbutz? For a resort hotel? It feels like a violation not just of people, but of the land itself. The Arab-Jews I grew up with—we knew that coexistence was possible. The story of Tantura tells me that here, in this new, old land, that possibility was burned down along with the houses of the village.
Yonatan: Coexistence? David, you are a good businessman but a poor historian. We extended our hand to the Arabs in '47. The Partition Plan gave them a state on half of

this land. Our "coexistence" was a willingness to compromise on our G-d-given inheritance. They refused. They chose war. Tantura was not an equal meeting of two tragic peoples. It was the logical outcome of that choice. It is the law of history. To the victor go the spoils, and the consequences of defeat. This sentimental mourning for "what was lost"... Tantura was a drop of water in an ocean. How much was lost by the Jews who fled or were expelled from the Old City of Jerusalem? From Gush Etzion? From the Jewish Quarter of Hebron, a place that had a continuous Jewish presence for millennia until *they* slaughtered *us* in '29? Where is your mourning for them, David? The Palestinians have cultivated their "Nakba" into a global brand, a weapon to delegitimize us. And people like you, and you Rahel, with your bleeding hearts, provide the ammunition. You look at one beach and you see a sin. I look at a map and I see a miracle of survival against impossible odds, secured by the very harshness you now condemn.
Rahel: And you, Yonatan, look at

the map and forget the people. The faces. This is not about "victors and spoils." That is the language of empires and Cossacks, not of the Judaism we came here to build. We did not come to create another nation of conquerors. We came to heal a broken world! *Tikkun Olam*! Did we forget that when the Alexandroni Brigade's soldiers lined men up against that village wall? Our strength as a people was always meant to be our moral clarity, our prophetic tradition. Tantura is a sign that we became that which we despised: a people who believes in the purity of force. A people who, in a moment of crisis, lost its soul.
Host: It seems that with every step forward in this conversation, you reveal a deep, and perhaps unbridgeable, fracture at the heart of your shared experience. But your lives continued. You all lived, had families, built careers. Let's move on from the battlefields and the bitter debates, to your lives in the later decades. The Six-Day War of 1967. Israel faced existential threats from three armies, and in six days, captured the Sinai, the Golan, the

West Bank, and, crucially for all of you, Jerusalem. Where were you in '67, and what did that stunning victory mean to your Israel?
Rahel: In 1967, I was in the Negev. A mother of three. Our kibbutz had grown from a few mud huts to a thriving agricultural community with a regional school that served dozens of settlements. The days before the war... were terrifying. The speeches from Cairo, from Amman, promising to push us into the sea. Nasser closing the Straits of Tiran. Our borders collapsing. The entire kibbutz was dug in. We had air raid shelters full of children and their books. I wasn't on the front line this time, but in the communications office, coordinating with the regional command, taking calls, watching the bulletins. The victory was... it was a revelation. It felt like God's hand. Not just surviving, but flourishing. We didn't just survive, we doubled our territory overnight. And most of all, Jerusalem was whole again. The Western Wall, in our hands! We felt the prayers of two thousand years answered. It was vindication. But a difficult one. Almost overnight,

our neighbor to the east, Jordan, became a population under our rule. I remember the debate on our kibbutz, that first week. "We have liberated our ancestors' land, but now we are occupiers of another people." That debate never ended. It started in June 1967 and continues to this day, in that very same dining hall. For me, the victory was the beginning of a much harder struggle: the struggle to live with our power. To be a Jewish state with control over millions of non-Jews. It was a test of our founding principles, and I'm not sure we've passed it. I have grandchildren now, some of whom live in settlements in the West Bank. We don't talk about politics at Shabbat dinner. It is too painful. The joy of '67 feels a very long time ago.
Yonatan: *Schmerzhaft*. The German word for painful. My feelings were painful. It was the ultimate "I told you so." I felt this profound, almost religious, sense of vindication, but it was laced with the bitterness of knowing we could have had it all in '48. Had Ben-Gurion and his coterie of socialists

not capitulated, we could have secured all of this without the bloodshed and terror of the preceding nineteen years. I was in Jerusalem on the eve of the war. I could feel it in the air. This time, there would be no restraint. This time, the IDF was not the Hagana of the '30s. It was a lion. When Paratrooper Commander Motta Gur announced on the radio, "The Temple Mount is in our hands!", I did not weep. I exhaled. For the first time since 1948, I felt the country was on a path my comrades and I had always envisioned. A path of strength. Of historical inevitability. I walked to the Western Wall. I saw the stunned, religious faces, weeping. And I saw my secular, fighter friends, stroking their chins in wonder. We had done it. We had erased the shame of 1948. The Left's panic afterward, their immediate hand-wringing about "occupation," confirmed everything I always believed about them. They were terrified of Jewish power. They preferred a small, besieged, morally pure state to a strong, historic Israel. That victory in '67 was my life's

work coming to fruition, even if it was done by men I despised. My life since has been about holding that ground. Physically and ideologically. To make sure the panic and weakness of the Left never gives back what we won, not in battle, but by an act of prophetic, historic right.
David: For my family and my community, '67 was a moment of immense, complex pride. For the first time, the Jewish state seemed truly powerful, truly secure from existential threat. For a community that had fled for its lives, this was a balm. A deep, deep healing. I was now a successful businessman in Tel Aviv. We watched the war on television, glued to the news broadcasts, our hearts in our throats. The pride was universal. We were all Israelis that week. We won. For the Mizrahi community, there was a special joy. The "wall" that had separated us from our Eastern homes, from the places our families had lived for centuries, was shattered in that lightning war. We were in Gaza. We were in the Sinai. For a brief time, for some of us, it was a reunion of sorts with the Arab world, just under a flag of victory

. But what it meant for the country's future... that was the problem. It brought into sharp relief a question we had been asking since 1951: which "us" were we? The state celebrated the "liberation" of Jerusalem's holy sites. But for many of us, who were Mizrahi, our heritage, our *Mizrach*, was in Baghdad, in Damascus, in Aleppo. The state's gaze was still to the West. Its symbols were still the kibbutz and the pioneer, its holy places were European-themed and built on sand. The '67 victory solidified this idea of a "Greater Israel," but it was a biblical, Euro-centric vision. Our culture, our music, the sounds of oud and kanun, was still the music of the periphery, the music of the development towns and the transit camps. The '67 victory was Israeli. The triumph that followed, the settling of the West Bank... that, my friend, was an Ashkenazi project. It was fueled by a religious-nationalist fervor that was alien to our community, and by a sense of destiny that we, who had just been stripped of our own destiny in Iraq, didn't share. I

dataFragment.data: . Which is why i have invited a scholar to discuss the haopenings at Tantura. Everyone please welcome Theodore Katz.

Please sir. Do not be nervous.
Endorphin: A man in his late sixties, with a gentle but firm face and tired, intellectual eyes, takes a seat at the table. He wears a simple tweed jacket and carries a worn leather briefcase. He nods courteously to the others.
Theodore: Thank you for having me. It is an honor. My name is Theodore Katz. I was a historian at the University of Haifa, and the author of the work... on Tantura.
Endorphin: Let us start at the beginning. Tell us a bit about yourself. Who are you and what connection brought you to the history of Tantura?
Theodore: (He takes off his glasses and cleans them with a handkerchief, a thoughtful, deliberate gesture) I am, or was, an Israeli historian. A son of this land. My parents came from Poland in the '30s, part of the Labor Zionist stream, like you, Rahel. I grew up on a kibbutz in the north, not unlike yours. I was taught the same myths, the same heroic narrative of the War of Independence. I fought in '67 and '73, in the armored corps

. I was a believer. My connection to Tantura began as a simple academic project. I was conducting research for my master's thesis on the role of the Alexandroni Brigade in the 1948 war, specifically on the battles in the Sharon region, including places just south of here. I came across Tantura in the official IDF archives. The reports spoke of a tough battle, but nothing seemed extraordinary. But then I started talking to veterans, off the record, at brigade reunions. One man mentioned "it got out of hand there." Another whispered that there was a "lot of shooting after the fight." A seed was planted. My project shifted. It became about finding out what really happened in that one small fishing village on a single night in May 1948. It became my life's work.
Endorphin: What did you find? Tell us about the process.
Theodore: It was... like being an archaeologist of memory. The official record was clean. But the human record was not. I conducted dozens of taped interviews with veterans of the Alexandroni Brigade. I spoke to Arab survivors from Tantura, now living in refugee camps in Jordan and the West Bank. I cross

-referenced testimonies. I used British maps, aerial photos from the time, diaries, letters. The picture that emerged was not of a simple, "clean" battle. It was of a village that surrendered. That offered no organized resistance. And then... there was a massacre. Not of combatants, but of civilians. Young men were separated from their families. They were shot. Some in a mass grave near the village cemetery, some near the beach. The number... that has become the political football. My research pointed to around two hundred killed. After the village was "cleared," the women, children, and elderly were expelled to the West Bank, and their homes were bulldozed or turned over to new Jewish immigrants. The location, that beautiful beach, was part of the land expropriated for Kibbutz Nahsholim. I corroborated the accounts from the Israeli veterans with the accounts from the Palestinian survivors. The details matched. The place where they said the bodies were buried, the descriptions of the soldiers, the timeline. There was no doubt in my mind, as an historian, that a war crime had been committed.
Endorphin: "War crime." That's a very charged phrase

, Yonatan. What about due process? Hearsay?
Yonatan: Hearsay? It is *all* hearsay! Twenty, thirty, forty years after the fact? Old men embellishing stories? Traumatized Arabs manufacturing a narrative for political gain? You call yourself a historian, but what you've done is propaganda. You took a collection of rumors, a handful of contradictory and emotionally charged statements from non-experts, and built them into an accusation! In a court of law, your case would be thrown out for lack of evidence. You have no bodies. You have no orders. You have no forensic proof. You have an agenda, sir. An agenda to vilify the state. And in doing so, you have handed a weapon to those who seek our destruction.
Theodore: (His voice remains calm, but there's a steely edge to it) My "agenda," Mr. ben Avraham, was the historical truth. The "due process" of academic history is different from that of a courtroom. It's the painstaking cross-corroboration of sources. I had over twenty taped testimonies from your own soldiers. Some were filled with remorse. Some were casual, almost boastful.

Only one said, "It was a fierce battle." The rest described a mop-up operation that turned into a slaughter. As for bodies, I found two IDF veterans who independently identified the same location for a mass grave, near the mosque. My request to have the site properly excavated was, as you know, denied by the authorities. The refusal to look is the most damning evidence of all. What is there to hide?
Rahel: Theodore... what you described... It breaks my heart. It breaks the story we told ourselves. But I also have to ask... what is the purpose of digging up this grave? What is the goal? Is it to heal? Or is it just to accuse? I see my grandsons in the IDF. I want them to be proud, and to be moral. How does your work help with that? Doesn't it just... pour acid on everything we've tried to build?
Theodore: Rahel, that is the hardest question. And it deserves an honest answer. My work is not about delegitimizing Israel. It is about making it more legitimate. A state that can confront its own past, that can admit its sins and reconcile with them, is a strong, mature,

and morally healthy state. A state that lives by myths and suppresses its own history is fragile and brittle. The purpose is to say to the Palestinians, "We see you. We acknowledge the suffering that was part and parcel of our birth." And to say to ourselves, "This is the cost of our state. We are no more pure than any other nation forged in blood." It is not to pour acid; it is to perform a necessary, painful surgery to remove a cancerous lie that has been festering at the heart of our national narrative for decades. The goal is reconciliation, not recrimination. But the first step to reconciliation is the truth.
David: As a man whose history was erased, I must side with the search for truth. My community's suffering, our being forced from our homes in Baghdad, is well documented. The property we left behind is a matter of record. Yet for years, the official Israeli story wanted to smooth over our pain, to pretend that our "absorption" was a simple, joyous event. It was not. We carry our wounds. So when I hear you, sir, Yonatan, dismiss the pain of another people because it's inconvenient... it angers me.

You talk of historic right. Is there no historic right for the people of Tantura? We, as Jews, should be the first to understand the pain of displacement. We should be the first to extend empathy. That you do not is a tragedy. Tantura, to me, is not just about Arabs and Jews. It is about the kind of people we become when we have power. We were victims for so long. I fear we learned only the lesson of the aggressor, not the lesson of the victim.
Yonatan: Empathy! Empathy is the luxury of the secure. You are secure in your villa in Tel Aviv, David. You are secure on your kibbutz, Rahel. I have never been secure. My entire life, I have seen the world arrayed against us. They see not the nuance you cherish, Theodore. They do not say, "Ah, an introspective Jewish state that admits its failings." They say, "Ah! Even they admit they are murderers! The whole enterprise is built on a lie!" You are not arming us with truth. You are loading their gun. You are giving them ammunition for their fight to push us into the sea.

You talk of reconciliation. Where is the Arab historian uncovering the massacres of Hebron? Safed? The Mufti's alliance with Hitler? Reconciliation requires two sides. They have offered nothing but denial and hatred for a hundred years. Your "truth" is a one-sided surrender. We did what we had to do, for our survival. The ends justify the means. It is the oldest and most honest law of war.
Rahel: And if you sacrifice all morality for the ends... what then have you become? When we were building the kibbutz, we had a principle that "the person is more important than the thing." Even in a hard time, even when we needed a tractor to work the fields, if a person was sick, the tractor waited. The person was paramount. Yonatan, your philosophy says the state is paramount, the survival is paramount, and the person—be it an Arab farmer or the moral soul of a Jewish soldier—is expendable. That is not a state I want to live in. That is not the "light unto the nations."
Endorphin: It seems Tantura serves as a proxy for the entire conflict. For some, a foundational sin to

be confessed. For others, a slander to be fought. Theodore, your work on Tantura cost you your university degree. It made you a pariah in many academic circles. Was it worth it?
Theodore: (He looks out at the sea for a long moment before answering) I live with that question every day. The lawsuit, the public vilification, the stripping of my MA... it was... crucifying. I lost friends. My career was shattered. But was it worth it? How can a historian ask that question? My duty is to the past, to the silent voices that were buried in that sand on the beach, both literally and figuratively. The personal cost... is regrettable. But it's secondary. Look, I don't enjoy this. I don't relish causing pain to good people like Rahel, or making enemies of patriots like Yonatan. But the alternative—remaining silent, participating in the lie—was a price my conscience could not pay. A society that destroys the man who speaks a difficult truth is a society that cannot face its future. So was it worth it? I believe that someday, when there is a true, lasting peace here, it will be built on

foundations like the ones I tried to lay. Small, painful, but solid. In that sense, yes. It was worth it.
David: I never understood that. The hostility to your work. For my community, the establishment has spent decades denying or downplaying our experience. Our persecution. The discrimination we faced. The story of "the first aliyah from the Arab countries was one of pure joy and relief" is a myth. A comforting lie for the Ashkenazim. But when we try to tell our true story, we are dismissed as bitter, as trying to create division. The state doesn't want messy history. It wants a clean, heroic narrative. You, Theodore, threatened that narrative. Just as we do when we speak of the racism we faced in the transit camps. Yonatan speaks of historical right, but the state's history is written by one group, for one group. We, the Mizrahim, are footnotes. And the Palestinians... they are erased entirely.
Yonatan: You see how insidious this is? David now equates the alleged killing of combatants in a captured village with… what? Rudeness at a government office? The state trying to forge a new Hebrew

-speaking Israeli culture? These things are not the same. They are not on the same moral plane. One is the brutal calculus of war; the other is the growing pains of a nascent nation. This is what your work does, Theodore. It provides the intellectual poison for people to conflate the existential actions of survival with the petty social grievances of assimilation. You create a false equivalence that hollows out the justification for the state itself. So no, it was not worth it. Not to Israel. It was a selfish act of academic vanity, and its price will be paid in the erosion of our national soul. The soul you claim to be healing, but are in fact mortally wounding.
Endorphin: We have moved from personal testimony to historical debate, from memory to its contested interpretation. This tension between the story a nation needs to survive and the history a scholar insists it must face… it is the heart of this conflict. I want to thank all of you for your honesty. There is one final, I think crucial, question. It is a simple one. When you are alone, and you think of the word "Israel"—what do you see?
(The three older Israelis and the historian are silent for a time

. The sun is lower now, gilding the water. The sound of the other patrons at the resort has faded into a soft murmur.)
Yonatan: I see the fortress. I see the walls around the Old City, now in Jewish hands. I see the Golan Heights, and how it protects the Galilee. I see the Iron Dome intercepting a rocket over Tel Aviv. I see the Menorah, but forged of iron and steel. I see a weapon, a shield, a refuge. Israel is not an abstract ideal. It is a lifeboat in a storm. It is the only place on earth where a Jewish soldier with a gun protects a Jewish child learning Torah. It is the promise that the fires of Europe and the hatred of Baghdad will never, ever again consume us. It is not gentle. It is not apologetic. It is strong. It is ours. And above all, it is permanent.
Rahel: I see a garden in the desert. The smell of orange blossoms in the Jezreel Valley. A classroom full of children from Russia, from Ethiopia, from Argentina, all learning to speak Hebrew. I hear the music of Naomi Shemer mixed with the
